Most people know wild sarsaparilla for one thing… old-fashioned root beer. 🍺🌿

But this fascinating woodland plant has so much more to its story.

It spreads through underground rhizomes, meaning an entire patch of plants may actually be one connected colony! Its fragrant roots have been traditionally used to flavour root beer and have a long history of use by Indigenous peoples and early settlers.

We can’t wait to make our wild root beer soap with it! 

Next time you’re walking through a shady forest, keep an eye out for its distinctive leaves and separate flower stalk—it might be one of the most interesting plants beneath your feet.

caption:
I’ve killed enough lavender plants to finally learn these 3 lessons the hard way. Especially when I start the plants from seed- it’s so much work to lose them. 

If you’re gardening in Zone 3 (I’m in Red Deer County) here’s what I wish I knew sooner:

❌ Mistake #1: Buying the wrong lavender.
Not all lavender is winter hardy. French and Spanish varieties may look beautiful at the garden centre, but they rarely survive our winters. Look for hardy English lavender like Munstead, Hidcote, or Phenomenal. I am now growing Munstead. 

❌ Mistake #2: Loving it too much.
Lavender hates wet feet. Heavy clay soil, low spots in the garden, and too much watering can quickly lead to root rot. Good drainage is everything. Lavender also loves full sun ☀️

❌ Mistake #3: Pruning in the fall.
I used to tidy mine up before winter. Big mistake. Fall pruning leaves tender growth exposed to freezing temperatures and can lead to winter kill. Wait until spring when new growth appears. Be sure to cover with a straw bale for extra winter protection! 

The funny thing about lavender is that it thrives on a little neglect. Give it sunshine, excellent drainage, and leave it alone more often than not. Learn from my mistakes.

Something I never thought I’d be saying is that there are more than 30,000 new faces around here since I last posted any type of introduction! That number still blows my mind if I’m being honest.

So hi, I’m Jess 👋🏼Mom, wife, retired nurse, nature lover, and owner of Prairie Soap Shack here in central Alberta. I started my business in 2019 when I was on mat leave and making soap in my kitchen after my family went to bed.

My nursing career and work in wound care served as the foundation for my interest in skin care, and once my love of nature and wild plants joined the party, there was no stopping.

When I’m not working, I’m often helping on the family farm, hanging out with my family and dog Ginny, taking my kids to hockey and other activities, or losing myself in a really good book. I spend time outside in all seasons, whether it’s hiking, canoeing, skiing, or foraging for the wild plants I use both in my business and my home!

caption:
Photo dump April 4/26. Our backcountry in the #reddeerrivervalley … did you know we live in a unique geological biome here. We have a mix of boreal, parkland and grasslands overlapping. I’m trying to research this more and learn about this. It fascinates me. 
In the warmer months (starting now), my family tries to get out here to explore once a week. We haven’t even scratched the surface of ground to explore - lots is inaccessible. But we find new game trails, try new things like tapping a birch tree, and I am forever looking at the ground- observing and memorizing the plants/lichens/mosses/grasses. 

Some things of interest we saw this particular day : a deer skull and skeleton, spruce tree damage from sapsuckers, a beaver slide by dam and tons of newly felled trees (major beaver activity), a huge granite rock with quartz veins in it, slimy bentonite clay on the badlands, a flying eagle overhead, ladybugs galore. The ground is slowly warming and waking up. We could hear streams rippling through the crevices as the snow melts and runs off and down towards the river. The river is still mostly iced over. 

#reddeerrivervalley #outdoorfamilies #spring

caption:
Wheat gum. Farmer’s gum. 
Have you chewed it before?

I’m sure it’s moments like these that will become core memories for our kids. Taking a scenic drive home from town so we can check crops, and have dad teach you how to grind up wheat in your hands… chew and chew till it turns into gum. Careful not to swallow the wheat, only your saliva … till it’s gum. Then I was picking wild Saskatoons … they added that in there and made Saskatoon gum! 

After years of making sourdough- I realized it’s gluten that forms and turns the wheat into a stretch “gum”. Science and nature are so cool. So are farmer dads. They’re cool too. ❤️😎
